processing: Bancha cut on the branch in early November and shade-dried is pan-roasted as needed, simmered in a kettle with dried tea flowers, then frothed in a tall bowl with a large whisk tipped with salt.
harvest_season: The bancha used for it is cut with the branches in early November in the Nita and Yasugi areas.
appearance_dry: Coarse shade-dried bancha leaf and twig, browned by pan-roasting, with dried tea flowers added.
appearance_liquor: An amber bancha brew under a pale layer of froth, with small pieces of food set into it.
appearance_wet: Large, soft brown bancha leaves and stems, left behind when the brew is poured.
taste_profile: A savoury snack more than a drink: toasty bancha softened by froth and a touch of salt, with rice, beans or simmered vegetables in each mouthful.

brewing.notes: Simmer a handful of bancha with five or six dried tea flowers, cool slightly, pour a little into a tall bowl and froth with a salted whisk. Add small bits of food and tap the bowl to shift them to one side.

vintage_note: Not a tea sold by vintage or season. It is a way of preparing local bancha, served as a regional speciality, and the leaf is cut once a year in early November and kept dried for use through the year.
description:
Botebote-cha is a dish you drink. It belongs to Izumo in Shimane and is one of Japan's furicha traditions, where coarse homemade tea is whisked to a froth. The name is said to come from the sound of the whisk.

The base is a rough local bancha, cut on the branch in early November, dried in the shade and pan-roasted when needed. It is simmered in a kettle with dried tea flowers, then a little is poured into a tall bowl and beaten with a big whisk whose tip has been touched with salt. It foams up much like matcha.

Into the foam go tiny portions of food: rice ball, red bean rice, boiled beans, shiitake, koya tofu, simmered mountain vegetables. There are no chopsticks. You tap the bowl to gather the food to one side and tip it all into your mouth, ideally in one go.

The flavour is not recorded in much detail, but expect what bancha and salt suggest: toasty, plain and savoury. Around Yatsuka, dried wild chrysanthemum goes into the pot, and the drink is called kiku-cha or fuku-cha.

If you want to try it at home, a pan-roasted bancha and a large whisk will get you close. Do not chase the delicacy of a ceremony bowl; a matcha whisk is smaller than the one used here.
history:
Its origin is uncertain, and three accounts circulate. One makes it a working meal for tatara ironworkers and fishermen on the Sea of Japan, another an emergency food during a famine under the lord Matsudaira Fumai, and a third a commoners' answer to the tea ceremony of the upper classes. An older name, oke-cha (bucket tea), points to everyday people.

The modern form dates to the early Showa period, when the mingei folk craft movement of Yanagi Soetsu helped revive it as an Izumo speciality. That is when it took the name botebote-cha and the chopstick-free way of eating.
